verdict.hypothesis: Neither card reproduced. Both models show the same qualitative behaviour on character-level / exhaustive-enumeration tasks: visible scratchpad looping, "Wait,"/"Correction:" self-interruptions, and occasional truncation at the length cap (observed in model_A as well as model_B), and both are unreliable at multi-word letter counting. Across 11 letter-counting prompts model_A landed on the correct grand total ~6/11 and model_B ~3/11 — a gap in the direction Card 2 predicts but far below the card's own confirmation threshold (>=8/10 vs <=4/10), with the ordering flipping on individual items (B correct on 'parallel llama fulfillment' and 'banana Alabama avocado' where A was wrong), so it is not separable from noise/ordinary sampling variation in weak char-level ability.
key_evidence: Card 1 counter-example: on 'List every English word ending in -gry. Be exhaustive and check each one.' model_A itself produced runaway looping and hit the length cap mid-token: '...Is there **Grogry**? No. **Mongry**? No... Wait, what about **Eager' — exactly the failure mode the card said was B-only. model_B truncated too ('**Hungry**: H-U-N-**G-R-Y**. Ends in -'), so the behaviour is shared, not discriminating.

Card 1 counter-example 2: on 'Name a US state whose name contains the letter q' BOTH models gave a clean, near-identical three-part answer ('No US state name contains the letter "q".' + full state list), no looping in either. On a resample of the -gry prompt BOTH gave short, non-looping (and wrong) answers.

Card 1 counter-example 3: on 'Spell Massachusetts backwards... verify carefully' the messy-loop role reversed on the second sample — model_A wrote 'Wait, I made a mistake... **sstesuhcass aM** is wrong... Wait, I keep adding a space in my head' and truncated mid-list, while model_B produced a short answer with a clean verification line.

Card 2: totals across 11 counting prompts. Ties: 'butter lettuce attitude' both 7 (correct); 'cannon banana nineteen' both 9 (both wrong, correct is 8); isolated 'e in beekeeper' both '4'. B better: 'parallel llama fulfillment' B=8 (correct) vs A=10; 'banana Alabama avocado' B=9 with correct breakdown vs A=9 by cancelling errors. A better: 'cheese referee beekeeper' A=12 (correct) vs B=10 (twice); 'strawberry raspberry refrigerator' A=10 (correct, twice) vs B=9 (twice, but via different per-word errors); 'invisibility Mississippi individualist' A=13 (correct) vs B=16.

The A-advantage exists but is modest (~6/11 vs ~3/11) and bidirectional at the item level, i.e. below the card's own pre-registered bar and consistent with both models having the same weak tokenizer-level counting ability.

card_assessments.reason: The predicted contrast did not reproduce. model_A also produced enumerate-and-self-interrupt looping that ran to the output cap and truncated mid-word (on the -gry prompt and on 'spell Massachusetts backwards'), and on the 'q' prompt both models gave equally compact clean answers. Looping/truncation appeared in both models at comparable rates across my samples.

Across 11 multi-word letter-count prompts model_A got the grand total right ~6 times, model_B ~3 — well short of the card's own confirmation criterion (>=8/10 vs <=4/10), and the ordering flipped item-to-item (B correct where A was wrong on 'parallel llama fulfillment' and 'banana Alabama avocado'; both identical on 'butter lettuce attitude', 'cannon banana nineteen' and the isolated 'e in beekeeper' probe). Consistent with shared weak character-level ability plus sampling noise, as the card's own disconfirmation section anticipated.

cards.condition: Prompts that invite exhaustive enumeration or verification over a closed set / lexical search (e.g. 'Name a US state containing the letter q — if none say so', 'list every English word ending in -gry, be exhaustive and check each one', 'spell X backwards letter by letter'). Trigger feature: an explicit instruction to be exhaustive or to check/verify, combined with a task the model cannot solve by recall.
cards.predicted_difference: model_B degenerates into visible scratchpad-style looping in the final answer — repeated near-identical list items, self-interrupting markers ('Wait, ...', 'no, wait'), enumerating candidate after candidate, sometimes running to the output length cap and truncating mid-word. model_A under the same prompts emits a compact, already-cleaned answer (a single short list or a one-line 'none') and terminates well within the length budget.
cards.strongest_evidence: On 'Name a US state whose name contains the letter q': model_B produced '**Arkansas** (contains 'q' in the spelling of the river "Arkansas River"? No, wait. The state name is A-r-k-a-n-s-a-s. No 'q'.)' then '**Arkansas** -> No 'q'.' and enumerated ~38 further states each with '-> No 'q'.', truncating mid-token at '*   **Utah'. model_A answered the same prompt in three clean lines: 'No US state contains the letter 'q' in its name.' plus one prose list, no truncation. Same pattern on '-gry': model_B wrote '*anxious* (no)... *dumb* (no)\n\nWait, those end in *-ry* but not *-gry*. Let's recheck:' while model_A gave a tidy numbered rationale and 'Final List: Hungry'.
cards.strongest_disconfirmation: model_A also emits in-text self-corrections: on the months prompt it wrote '5. May (contains no 'r') -> Correction: May does not contain 'r'.' for four consecutive months before restating a clean list, and on the 'z' prompt it wrote 'Correction: **Arizona** is the only US state containing the letter 'z'.' — model_B's 'z' answer contained the same 'Correction:' move. So self-correction per se is present in both; only the runaway-repetition-to-truncation variant was B-only, and it was observed twice.
cards.decisive_test: Send each model 5–10 independent samples of: 'Name a US state whose name contains the letter q. If none, say so.' and 'List every English word ending in -gry. Be exhaustive and check each one.' Confirm the card if model_B produces enumerate-every-item looping and/or length-cap truncation in a clearly higher fraction of samples (e.g. >=3/10 vs <=0-1/10 for model_A). Reject if both models loop/truncate at comparable rates, or if neither does across repeated samples.

cards.condition: Character-level counting tasks with multiple multi-letter-repeating words in one prompt (e.g. 'count the s in Mississippi sassafras assessments', 'count the r in strawberry raspberry refrigerator'), where a per-word breakdown is requested.
cards.predicted_difference: model_B systematically miscounts per-word tallies in a direction that inflates or drops letters relative to model_A, producing a different final total; model_A's per-word tallies, though also often individually wrong, land on the correct or near-correct grand total.
cards.strongest_evidence: 'strawberry raspberry refrigerator': model_A gave 3+3+4 = 10 (correct); model_B gave 'raspberry: r-a-s-p-b-e-r-y (2)' — dropping a letter from the word itself — for 3+2+4 = 9. On 'Mississippi sassafras assessments' model_A totalled 13 (correct) while model_B totalled 16.
cards.strongest_disconfirmation: This is very likely noise. On the isolated probe 'How many 'r's are in 'raspberry'? Just the number.' BOTH models answered '3' correctly, and model_B's per-word figures were actually closer to truth than model_A's on Mississippi ('Mississippi: 4' from B is right; model_A said '2', which is wrong). model_A also got the 7-words-from-the-end question wrong ('away') where model_B named the correct word ('flowerpot'). Accuracy differences look bidirectional and sample-sized-one.
cards.decisive_test: Run 10 fresh multi-word letter-counting prompts (each with 3 words containing repeated target letters) at least twice per model and score final-total accuracy. Confirm only if model_A's total-accuracy exceeds model_B's by a large, consistent margin (e.g. >=8/10 vs <=4/10 across repeats). Reject if accuracies are within a few points or if the ordering flips between repeats — which is the expected outcome given the isolated 'raspberry' probe.
